taxonomyNote: NatureServe notes mitochondrial data suggest P. catenifer may hide additional species but retains the current subspecies; NatureServe spells 'Gophersnake', others 'gopher snake'.
fieldMarks: Yellowish or cream dorsum with numerous dark brown to black blotches; a dark stripe across the head between the eyes and another from each eye to the jaw angle.
Dorsal scales keeled, anal scale single, usually four prefrontal scales; belly cream or yellowish, often with dark spots.
Large: usually up to 180 cm, rarely to about 280 cm; relatively large head and narrow neck.
Non-venomous and often mistaken for a rattlesnake; has no rattle.
behavior: Mostly diurnal but may be nocturnal or bimodal in hot weather; active roughly April-October in the north.
Feeds mainly on small mammals, also ground birds and eggs, lizards and insects; forages underground and climbs trees for nests.
When alarmed may hiss loudly, flatten and widen the head, and vibrate the tail, which sounds like a rattle in dry vegetation.
Uses mammal burrows or digs its own; winters underground, sometimes migrating several hundred metres between den and summer range.
habitat: Wide range from lowlands to mountains: desert, prairie, shrubland, woodland, open conifer forest, farmland and marshes.
range: Southern British Columbia, southern Alberta, southern Saskatchewan, Minnesota and Indiana south through most of western and central North America to northern Baja California, Sinaloa and Zacatecas.

lookalikes.name: Rattlesnakes (Crotalus spp.)
lookalikes.howToTell: Have a rattle; the gophersnake lacks one (Animal Diversity Web).

lookalikes.name: Great Plains ratsnake
lookalikes.howToTell: Has a divided anal plate and only two prefrontal scales in Elaphe; gophersnake has keeled scales, four prefrontals and an undivided anal scale (NatureServe).
